Chapter 11: Facing the Truth—Memory, Responsibility, and Hope.
Coming to terms with the history of segregation isn’t easy, is it? It means facing some uncomfortable truths, questioning what we’ve always been told, and realizing that the world we live in today was shaped by choices—even by people we never met.
Picture a teacher, standing in front of her class, trying to explain why her students’ lives are so different—even though their homes are just a few miles apart. Or think about a city official, staring at old maps, seeing the dividing lines that split neighborhoods, and asking himself what it would take to heal those wounds. Then there’s a family searching for a new home, only to face the same barriers their grandparents did. You have to wonder—will things ever really change?
Facing the truth can be painful. But you know what? It’s also necessary. Because when we open that door, even just a crack, we start to see new possibilities—a chance to make different choices this time around.
Some communities have started to do just that. They’re holding public hearings, putting up memorials, even talking about reparations for those who were harmed. These steps might feel small, but they matter. They show us the story isn’t finished yet—and maybe, just maybe, the future doesn’t have to repeat the past.
Most folks don’t even know where to start. The problems look huge, and history can feel like a weight that’s just too heavy to lift. But change really begins with honesty—with the courage to look at the world as it is, and the imagination to picture what it could become.
